Chapter 9: Designing for Error and Recovery
Let’s be real—no matter how much care goes into designing something, people are always going to find ways to make mistakes. We’re creative, we get distracted, and sometimes... we just do the unexpected. The real goal isn’t to wipe out every possible error, but to make sure it’s easy to bounce back when they happen—and that the consequences aren’t a big deal.
One of the big ideas here is something called error forgiveness. Imagine you’re working on a document and you hit the wrong button. If there’s an “undo” option, you can just relax and fix it, right? That little safety net encourages you to try new things, knowing you can always go back if you mess up. Or picture a website that saves your drafts automatically—so even if your browser crashes, your hard work isn’t lost forever.
There’s also the concept of graceful degradation. Think about those times when your Wi-Fi drops or the power flickers out. A well-designed system will hang on to as much of your progress as possible, and help you pick up right where you left off. Like, if your phone loses signal during a download, but then picks up again and finishes it once you reconnect. Or a form that remembers what you typed, even if the page reloads.
And let’s talk about error messages. They shouldn’t sound like a robot scolding you. Instead, they’re a chance to offer support. A message like, “Please enter a valid email address,” is way more helpful than something mysterious like, “Error 404.” It’s about explaining what went wrong—and, more importantly, how to fix it.
So, what are some practical ways to design for error and recovery? Here are a few that really make a difference:
First, give people undo and redo options—that way, if someone makes a mistake, they can easily reverse it.
Add confirmation prompts before anything that can’t be undone. Think of that little “Are you sure?” box before you delete a file.
Use automatic saving to keep work safe, even if something unexpected happens.
And finally, make sure your error messages are clear and supportive, so people always know what went wrong and how to move forward.
When you design with these ideas in mind, you’re not just making things safer—you’re helping people feel more confident and empowered. Mistakes are just part of being human. By embracing them, designers create products that are resilient, supportive, and honestly, just a whole lot nicer to use.
